## ARGUMENT

### An employer that fails to engage in the interactive process is liable under the ADA when that failure prevents identification of a reasonable accommodation.

The ADA makes it discrimination to fail to make reasonable accommodations to the known limitations of a qualified individual with a disability, absent undue hardship. 42 U.S.C. § 12112(b)(5)(A). The regulations contemplate that, to determine the appropriate accommodation, the employer may need to initiate an informal, interactive process with the employee. 29 C.F.R. § 1630.2(o)(3). This Court has long treated that process as the means by which the statutory duty is carried out. *Beck v. Univ. of Wis. Bd. of Regents*, 75 F.3d 1130, 1135–37 (7th Cir. 1996); *Gile v. United Airlines, Inc.*, 95 F.3d 492, 498–99 (7th Cir. 1996).

**A. The governing rule.** Liability attaches when the employer's failure to engage in the interactive process causes the failure to identify a reasonable accommodation. *Beck* held that an employer who fails to engage in good faith cannot escape liability if the process, properly pursued, would have uncovered a reasonable accommodation. 75 F.3d at 1135–37. The Court has repeated the rule consistently. *EEOC v. Sears, Roebuck & Co.*, 417 F.3d 789, 805–07 (7th Cir. 2005); *Jackson v. City of Chicago*, 414 F.3d 806, 813 (7th Cir. 2005); *Basden v. Prof'l Transp., Inc.*, 714 F.3d 1034, 1037–38 (7th Cir. 2013); *Kauffman v. Petersen Health Operations, LLC*, 769 F.3d 958, 963 (7th Cir. 2014).

The Court has also clarified that the failure to engage is not an independent source of liability. The employee must show that the breakdown prevented an accommodation that would have been available. *Rehling v. City of Chicago*, 207 F.3d 1009, 1015–16 (7th Cir. 2000); *Basden*, 714 F.3d at 1038. This is a causation requirement. It does not excuse the employer's own default. Where the employer's inaction is what left the accommodation question unanswered, the employer cannot rely on that gap to defeat the claim. *Sears*, 417 F.3d at 806–07.

**B. The employer bears responsibility for the breakdown when it fails to respond to the employee's notice.** An employee need not use particular words or propose a specific accommodation. The employer must have notice of the disability and the employee's desire for accommodation. Once it does, the employer must make a reasonable effort to understand the employee's limitations and explore options. *Bultemeyer v. Fort Wayne Cmty. Schs.*, 100 F.3d 1281, 1285–86 (7th Cir. 1996). An employer that meets an imprecise or incomplete request with silence, or demands that the employee name the perfect solution, has not participated in good faith. *Id.*; *Beck*, 75 F.3d at 1135–36. When the record shows that the employer caused the breakdown, responsibility for it rests with the employer. *Id.*; *Ekstrand v. Sch. Dist. of Somerset*, 583 F.3d 972, 976–77 (7th Cir. 2009).

**C. Application.** [Plaintiff] notified [Employer] of [his/her] limitations and [his/her] need for accommodation on [date]. [Employer] did not [respond / meet with Plaintiff / seek medical clarification / discuss alternatives]. Instead, it [describe conduct]. Under *Bultemeyer*, [Employer] could not rest on the supposed vagueness of Plaintiff's request. It was obliged to engage, and its failure to do so left unexplored the very options the process exists to surface.

Plaintiff has also shown that a reasonable accommodation was available. [Identify accommodations, e.g., modified schedule, reassignment to a vacant position, equipment, or leave], each of which was feasible and would have enabled Plaintiff to perform the essential functions of the job. *See Rehling*, 207 F.3d at 1015–16; *Jackson*, 414 F.3d at 813. Because [Employer]'s refusal to engage is the reason these options were never evaluated, the causal link *Beck* and *Basden* require is satisfied. At a minimum, the record presents genuine disputes of material fact as to who caused the breakdown and whether a reasonable accommodation existed. *See Gile*, 95 F.3d at 499; *Sears*, 417 F.3d at 807.

The district court's contrary conclusion rests on treating the interactive process as optional, or on faulting Plaintiff for a breakdown that [Employer] caused. Neither position is consistent with this Court's precedent. The judgment should be reversed.
